beats.intro: Lesson ten. [[sub]]Two kinds of power, and the three stages of a good decision.
beats.range: Managers rarely decide alone, but they take part in a great many decisions. [[big]]Some are profound: buy a building or lease it, borrow or sell shares. [[mid]]Some are personal: a seven or a twelve percent raise. [[tech]]Some are deeply technical, or legal. [[small]]And some are trivial: free drinks at the holiday party?
beats.power: In traditional industries, the person who made a decision was the person in a certain box on the org chart. [[pos]]Authority went with position. [[know]]A know-how business has a second kind of power: knowledge. [[split]]And because the knowledge the business runs on changes fast, the two kinds of power drift apart.
beats.obsolete: Picture a new engineering graduate. [[grad]]On day one she is fully up to date: lots of knowledge power, little position power. [[rise]]As she is promoted, her position power grows, [[fade]]while her grip on current technology fades. In Grove's words, we managers get a little more obsolete every day. [[gap]]The faster the technology or the customers change, the wider the gap. [[mesh]]The middle manager's job is to make the two kinds of power mesh.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which kind of power?
beats.model: Grove's ideal decision process has three stages. [[free]]Free discussion. [[clear]]A clear decision. [[supp]]And full support. [[loop]]And if the decision turns out to be wrong, you go back to free discussion and start again.
beats.free: First, free discussion: every view and every aspect, openly debated. [[heat]]The more heated the issue, the more the word free matters. [[hang]]In practice, people often hang back, sense which way the wind blows, and back the likely winner. [[car]]One car company even told a departing executive that people who did well there waited for their bosses' view, and then supported it. [[bad]]That produces bad decisions, because what the knowledgeable people know never reaches the table.
beats.clear: Second, a clear decision. [[heat]]Again, the more controversy, the more the word clear matters. [[fog]]Our instinct is the opposite: to blur a controversial decision and avoid an argument. [[later]]But that only postpones the argument, [[mad]]and people who dislike a decision are angrier still if they don't get a prompt, straight story.
beats.support: Third, full support. [[agree]]That does not mean agreement. [[diff]]Even with the same facts and the same goals, honest people disagree, and no amount of time will fix that on every issue. [[commit]]An organization does not live by agreement. It lives by people committing to support its decisions. [[expect]]That commitment you can, and must, get from everyone.
beats.who: This model comes easily to two groups. [[senior]]Senior managers who have been around long enough to feel at home with how things are done. [[grads]]And new graduates, because it is how lab partners settle their differences. [[mid]]Middle managers find it harder: [[h1]]stating views forcefully, [[h2]]making unpleasant decisions, [[h3]]and above all, backing a decision they argued against. [[win]]In time, the logic wins them over.
beats.lowest: Make each decision at the lowest competent level, [[close]]where people are closest to the situation and know the most. [[know]]And knowing means more than technical expertise. [[bruise]]It means expertise tempered by judgment, earned from the bruises of putting knowledge to work. [[mix]]If no one has both, build the best mix: Intel often invited someone more senior, for experience. [[equal]]But during free discussion, everyone speaks as an equal, whatever their rank.
beats.equal: A journalist once asked Grove whether Intel's informal dress, open partitions, and lack of reserved parking were just affectation. [[surv]]His answer: not affectation, survival. [[mix]]Every day, knowledge-power people and position-power people have to make decisions together. [[status]]Status symbols block the flow of ideas, facts and views. [[nec]]What looks like style is really necessity.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Position power and knowledge power drift apart; managers must make them mesh. [[w2]]Good decisions go through free discussion, a clear decision, and full support. [[w3]]Support means commitment, not agreement. [[w4]]Decide at the lowest competent level, mixing expertise and judgment. [[w5]]In discussion, everyone speaks as an equal. Now the lesson practice.
